messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 29
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Shopowner
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Vignette:
Arjun Patel was 29 when he came for treatment, a South Asian American man who ran a small convenience shop with his girlfriend of the past year. He described the trauma as physical abuse in a previous romantic relationship, something he had spent a long time trying to speak about as little as possible. When he finally recounted it, he did so in a flat, controlled voice that broke only when he reached the parts that still seemed to arrive in him as if they were happening in the present. Near the end of that relationship, an argument in their apartment had turned violent. What stayed with him most sharply was how quickly the room changed from ordinary conversation into danger. They had been talking about the relationship in a way that at first sounded familiar, the same kinds of charged topics that had led to fights before, and then his partner moved close, shouting into his face. Arjun remembered the smell of sweat, heavy and immediate in the small room, and then being grabbed and hit. He remembered freezing for a moment when he believed he should have defended himself or left sooner. That split second became, in his mind, proof of something terrible about him.

In the weeks afterward, he found that the memory did not remain in the past. It could come to mind suddenly, complete and forceful, without any sense that he had chosen to think about it. Sometimes it was a full memory brought on instantly by something around him before he even understood what had set it off. A customer leaning too close across the counter after rushing in from the summer heat, the smell of body odour in the narrow aisle, or even hearing a couple in the store drift into a tense conversation about trust or cheating could make the whole event surge back. At other times there was no clear picture at all. He would just feel the same terror and pressure in his chest, the same flood of emotion, as if his body had already recognized danger before his mind caught up. What unsettled him most was that his body seemed to react on its own. He had come to believe that his body was now an enemy of sorts, launching him into alarm even when he knew, rationally, that he was standing in his own shop in the middle of the afternoon.

When the memory came with more detail, rage came with it too. He did not describe fear first; he described heat, tension, and a violent anger that made his jaw lock and his hands shake. He hated feeling that anger, especially in public, and hated even more that it arrived tied to the same memory of not having done more. He was certain he should have stopped it, pushed back harder, left earlier, called for help, done something other than freeze. “I can’t rely on myself,” he said more than once, not as a dramatic statement but as a conclusion he felt he had earned. For Arjun, the worst part was not only that the assault had happened, but that in the crucial moment he had not been the person he thought he should be.

These reactions became woven into the routines of his days at the shop. He grew tense when strangers approached him, even in ordinary interactions that used to feel harmless: someone stepping too quickly up to the register, a man asking a question from too close by the cigarette case, a customer lingering near the counter while trying to make conversation. He watched people’s movements carefully and found himself bracing before he even knew why. By night this became more pronounced. Closing the shop after dark was especially difficult. He would check the lock repeatedly, look through the front window at people passing outside, and feel far less safe than he did during the day. Sleep became unreliable. He had trouble falling asleep, and if he woke in the night he stayed alert for long stretches, as though rest itself were unsafe.

Over time, he narrowed his world in practical ways. He asked his current partner to handle more evening shifts and avoided conversations, at work and at home, that even brushed against relationship conflict. He was not doing this casually; in his mind, certain topics carried the charge of the night everything changed. This avoidance strained things between them. She experienced him as shutting down or changing the subject abruptly, and he felt ashamed that he could manage inventory, suppliers, and customers but could not trust himself in an argument or even in a difficult discussion.

What brought him to treatment was not one dramatic collapse but the accumulation of this daily life. A customer had come in after work, sweaty and agitated, and while speaking sharply on the phone about his girlfriend he stepped close to the counter. Arjun felt the full force of the memory hit without warning and then a wave of rage so intense he had to leave the register and lock himself in the stockroom until his partner arrived. He was frightened by how quickly he could be pulled out of the present, and by how little faith he had in his own reactions afterward. Coming to therapy, what he wanted most was to stop living as though danger could arrive in any ordinary moment. What frightened him most was the possibility that this was now who he was: a man who could not rely on his own mind, his own body, or himself when it mattered.
